title: Discovery of the Higgs boson at CERN
summary: On 4 July 2012, at a seminar at CERN near Geneva, the ATLAS and CMS experiments presented preliminary results from the Large Hadron Collider showing a new particle with a mass around 125–126 GeV, at a level of 5 sigma. It appeared to be the Higgs boson, the missing piece of the Standard Model of particle physics. François Englert and Peter Higgs won the 2013 Nobel Prize in Physics for the theory it confirmed.

uncertainty.note: Announced at a scientific seminar at CERN on 4 July 2012.

as_recorded.value: Geneva, 4 July 2012. At a seminar held at CERN 1 today as a curtain raiser to the year’s major particle physics conference, ICHEP2012 in Melbourne, the ATLAS and CMS experiments presented their latest preliminary results in the search for the long-sought Higgs particle. Both experiments observe a new particle in the mass region around 125-126 GeV.
In 2012, their ideas were confirmed by the discovery of a so called Higgs particle at the CERN laboratory outside Geneva in Switzerland.

where.modern_name: CERN (European Organization for Nuclear Research), Route de Meyrin, Meyrin, Geneva, Switzerland
where.historical_name: CERN (European Organization for Nuclear Research), Meyrin, Canton of Geneva, Switzerland

importance.justification: Confirmed the predicted particle at the heart of the theory of how particles acquire mass, the missing piece of the Standard Model.

sources.title: CERN experiments observe particle consistent with long-sought Higgs boson
The Nobel Prize in Physics 2013 – Press release

reviewer_note: CERN labelled the July 2012 results preliminary and described the particle as consistent with the Higgs boson. The Nobel press release later treated the discovery as confirmed. The Standard Model is not the final theory of nature.
